canonical_topic: Global coal reserve geography and Atlantic vs. Pacific trade markets
definition: World coal reserves are concentrated in the Northern Hemisphere (notably the U.S. and Siberia), with relative scarcity in Western Europe, South America, and Africa; because transport cost is such a large share of coal's delivered cost, international trade splits into an Atlantic market and a larger Pacific market.
core_idea: About 80% of coal produced worldwide is consumed near its mine, and the high relative cost of transport divides the remaining international trade into two separate regional markets, with the Pacific market handling roughly two-thirds of global coal trade.
key_points: Coal reserves are concentrated in the Northern Hemisphere, particularly the United States and Siberia
Western Europe, South America, and Africa have relatively little coal
About 80 percent of coal produced worldwide is used close to where it is mined
High transportation cost as a share of total coal cost splits international trading into an Atlantic market and a Pacific market
Atlantic market importers include the United Kingdom, Germany, and Spain
Pacific market importers include Japan, Korea, and parts of China
About two-thirds of international coal trading occurs in the Pacific market
relationships: Explains why coal transportation/location trading is limited compared to natural gas
trading_implications: Regional split means coal trading strategies must be regionally specific (Atlantic vs. Pacific) rather than globally unified
